# Introduction to Ezekiel

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of Ezekiel

1. Yahweh calls Ezekiel to speak his words (1:1–3:27)
2. Yahweh judges Judah and Jerusalem (4:1–24:27)
3. Ezekiel prophesies against nearby nations (25:1–32:32)
4. Yahweh explains the fall of Jerusalem (33:1–33)
5. Ezekiel brings messages of hope (34:1–48:35)
    A. A new shepherd (34:1–31)
    B. Edom destroyed (35:1–15)
    C. Israel restored (36:1–37:28)
    D. Gog and Magog (38:1–39:29)
    E. Jerusalem and the temple restored (40:1–48:35)

### What is Ezekiel about?

The book of Ezekiel contains words that Ezekiel prophesied between 592 B.C. and 573 B.C. The Jewish people were exiled in Babylonia. Ezekiel told them that God had punished them because they sinned against him. However, Ezekiel assured them that God would restore them. God was using Babylon to punish them. But eventually another nation would defeat the Babylonians. Ezekiel also prophesied about how God will restore Jerusalem and the temple so that the people can worship and sacrifice to him again. Ezekiel then described how the land will be divided again among the tribes of Israel.

### How should the title of this book be translated?

“Ezekiel” or “The Book of Ezekiel” is the traditional name for this book. Translators may also call it “The Messages from God Brought by Ezekiel.”

### Who wrote the book of Ezekiel?

Ezekiel wrote the prophecies in the book of Ezekiel. He was a prophet and priest who lived near Babylon in the time of the exile.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### What was Ezekiel’s temple?

Several chapters of the book of Ezekiel give instructions about building a new temple. However, this temple is not the same as the temple the people would build after going back to Jerusalem. Because Ezekiel’s temple has never been built, some scholars think that this temple is to be built in the future. Other scholars think that Ezekiel’s temple is symbolic of the Church.

### Do the sacrifices in Ezekiel follow the law of Moses?

The sacrifices in Ezekiel 46 are somewhat different than the required sacrifices in Numbers 28. This may be because Ezekiel prophesied about a new temple with new sacrifices.

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### How should one represent Ezekiel’s visions in translation?

The book of Ezekiel has many complicated visions. Some are similar to passages in other Scripture books that describe future events. Some of these visions are about God rescuing Israel in the distant future.

It is unclear whether Ezekiel actually traveled to the particular places named in the visions, or whether what he described were mental ideas. For this reason, Ezekiel’s viewpoint is sometimes difficult to understand, even though the meanings of the visions may be clear.

Translators should avoid trying to explain these visions in their translations. Instead, they should present the visions just as they are in the source text.

### What does “know that I am Yahweh” mean?

This is a common phrase in the book of Ezekiel. It is meant to assure the reader that these messages truly came from God, and that he will do what he has promised. Translate this phrase consistently throughout the book.

### “son of man”

The phrase “son of man” translates simply to “mortal man” or “human being,” reminding Ezekiel that despite receiving extraordinary divine visions, he remains a creature dependent on God. By repeatedly calling Ezekiel this throughout this book, Yahweh establishes a clear boundary between his infinite glory and the messenger’s earthly limitations.

### “spirit,” “breath,” or “wind”

The same Hebrew word can mean either “spirit,” “breath,” or “wind.” In biblical times, the concept of a person’s spirit was closely related to the concept of a person’s breath. The term can also refer to wind, that is, the movement of air in the natural world.

# Ezekiel 2 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Yahweh calls Ezekiel to speak to rebellious Israel (1–5)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### A house of rebellion

Yahweh repeatedly calls Israel “a house of rebellion,” picturing the people as a household marked by refusal to obey him.

# Ezekiel 3 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter completes the commissioning of Ezekiel that began in chapter 2, and it ends with the prophet confined to his house and unable to speak unless Yahweh gives him a message.

1. Yahweh commissions Ezekiel as a watchman (1–11)
2. Yahweh’s Spirit strengthens and guides Ezekiel (12–15)
3. Yahweh holds Ezekiel responsible for warning the wicked (16–21)
4. Yahweh reveals his glory and commands Ezekiel to speak (22–27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Eating the scroll

Yahweh commands Ezekiel to eat a scroll, and it tastes as sweet as honey. This symbolic act represents the prophet taking Yahweh’s message into himself, so that the words he speaks are Yahweh’s words and not his own.

### The prophet as a watchman

A watchman guarded an ancient city by looking out for danger and warning the people. In the same way, Ezekiel must warn the people of Yahweh’s judgment, and Yahweh holds him accountable for the death of anyone whom he fails to warn.

# Ezekiel 4 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh commands Ezekiel to perform a series of symbolic actions that portray the coming siege of Jerusalem and the famine that will accompany it.

1. Yahweh commands Ezekiel to portray Jerusalem’s siege (1–3)
2. Ezekiel bears Israel’s guilt and judgment (4–8)
3. Ezekiel portrays the famine and suffering of Jerusalem (9–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel does not merely announce the siege of Jerusalem; he acts it out with a brick, an iron griddle, and his own body. Such enacted signs were a recognized form of prophecy and were understood to portray what Yahweh was about to do.

### Bearing iniquity

When Ezekiel “carries the iniquity” of Israel and of Judah, he is not being punished for his own sin. He is publicly representing the guilt of the people and the punishment that it deserves.

### Unclean food

The law of Moses forbade certain foods and required that food be prepared in ways that kept a person ritually pure. Baking bread over human excrement would defile both the food and the prophet, which is why Ezekiel protests in [4:14](../04/14.md).

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Instructions to Ezekiel

Yahweh gives most of his instructions in this chapter with a Hebrew verb form that the ULT renders as “you shall.” These are instructions rather than predictions. Translate this form with the most natural way in your language for giving instructions.

### Weights and measures

# Ezekiel 5 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter completes the series of symbolic actions that began in chapter 4 and then interprets them.

1. Yahweh judges Jerusalem for its rebellion (1–4)
2. Yahweh declares judgment because of Jerusalem’s abominations (5–10)
3. Yahweh brings famine, death, and scattering upon Jerusalem (11–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel acts out the coming judgment rather than only announcing it. Shaving the head and beard was in itself a sign of mourning and humiliation, and each portion of the hair stands for a group of the people, as Yahweh explains in [5:12](../05/12.md).

### Defiling the sanctuary

Yahweh gives as a reason for this judgment that the people have brought detestable things into his temple. To make the sanctuary unclean was to treat as common the one place that Yahweh had set apart for himself.

### The curses of the covenant

Famine, the sword, plague, wild animals, and parents eating their own children are the very punishments that Yahweh had warned of in the law of Moses if his people broke the covenant. The first hearers would have recognized these disasters as covenant curses rather than as random calamities.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Shifting addressees

Yahweh addresses Ezekiel in verses 1–4 with a singular “you.” From verse 7 on, he addresses the city of Jerusalem and its people, and the “you” is sometimes singular and sometimes plural, occasionally within a single verse. You may need to make the addressee explicit, as the UST does.

### Quotations within quotations

The whole chapter is speech that Yahweh makes to Ezekiel, and within it he repeatedly introduces further quoted speech with “Thus says the Lord Yahweh.” If these nested quotations would be confusing, you could translate the inner quotations as indirect speech.

### Expressions for anger

The ULT preserves the Hebrew words for anger literally, speaking of Yahweh’s “nose” and his “heat” in [5:13](../05/13.md) and [5:15](../05/15.md). Many languages will need ordinary words for anger and wrath here, as the UST has.

# Ezekiel 6 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter Yahweh tells Ezekiel to prophesy against the mountains of Israel, where the people worshiped idols.

1. Judgment on the places of idol worship (1–7)
    1. Yahweh commands Ezekiel to speak to the mountains of Israel (1–3)
    2. Yahweh will destroy the altars and leave the dead lying in front of the idols (4–7)
2. Some people will survive and remember Yahweh in exile (8–10)
3. Ezekiel is to lament over Israel’s coming destruction (11–14)
    1. The people will die by sword, famine, and plague (11–12)
    2. The dead will lie among the idols, and the land will become desolate (13–14)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### High places

The high places were hilltop sites where the Israelites built altars and set up idols to worship. Yahweh addresses the mountains, hills, stream beds, and valleys because that is where this idol worship took place, and he will defile those sites with the bodies of the people who worshiped there.

### Idolatry as prostitution

In [6:9](../06/09.md) Yahweh speaks of the people’s idol worship as if it were prostitution, that is, sexual unfaithfulness to him. This comparison appears often in Ezekiel.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh speaks to Ezekiel, telling him to speak to the mountains, and in that speech Ezekiel quotes Yahweh, who again tells Ezekiel what to say, so the chapter has up to four levels of quotation. See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]] for ways to make this clear.

### The identity of “you”

In verses 2 and 3, Yahweh tells Ezekiel to address his prophecy to the mountains of Israel. In verse 3, he begins speaking to the mountains using a plural “you” and “your.” The real audience for the prophecy is, of course, the people of Israel, and by verse 8 “you” has to refer to the people, so the two “audiences” have become blended. To make this clearer, you may wish to have “you” refer to the people throughout the chapter, as in the UST.

### “You will know that I am Yahweh”

This statement recurs throughout the chapter and the book. It means that when Yahweh carries out his judgment, the people will recognize that he is the true God who has all power and who does what he says. Translate it the same way each time it occurs.

Alternate translation: [And Yahweh spoke a message to me, saying]

# Ezekiel 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a prophecy in poetic language announcing that the end has come for the land of Israel.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to announce the end of the land of Israel (1–4)
2. The day of judgment is coming (5–13)
    1. The end has come because of the people’s ways (5–9)
    2. The day has arrived, and buying and selling will no longer matter (10–13)
3. The people will be helpless and will mourn (14–18)
4. Their wealth will not save them, and foreigners will defile Yahweh’s temple (19–22)
5. Yahweh will bring the nations, and no leader will be able to help (23–27)

Some translations set lines of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [7:2–27](../07/02.md).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The day of Yahweh

Throughout this chapter, “the end,” “the time,” and “the day” refer to the time when Yahweh will punish the people of Israel for their sins.

### Mourning practices

In this culture, people expressed grief by wearing sackcloth and shaving their heads (v. 18). Ezekiel uses these practices to show how the people will mourn when Yahweh judges them.

### Ritual uncleanness

In verses 19–20, Yahweh compares the people’s silver and gold to the impurity of menstruation. Under the law of Moses, menstruation made a person ritually unclean as well as physically unclean, so the comparison shows that the people will regard their wealth as something that kept them from God and therefore as something detestable to be thrown away.

# Ezekiel 20 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh refuses to let the elders of Israel inquire of him and instead has Ezekiel recount Israel’s long history of rebellion, followed by a promise of judgment and restoration.

1. The elders come to inquire of Yahweh, and he refuses them (1–4)
2. Yahweh recounts Israel’s rebellion against him (5–29)
    1. In Egypt (5–9)
    2. The first generation in the wilderness (10–17)
    3. The second generation in the wilderness (18–26)
    4. In the land Yahweh gave them (27–29)
3. Yahweh condemns the idolatry of the present generation (30–32)
4. Yahweh promises to judge his people and bring them back to their land (33–44)
5. Yahweh’s message against the forest of the south (45–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Acting for the sake of his name

Yahweh repeatedly holds back his punishment so that his name, meaning his reputation, would not be profaned among the nations who had seen him rescue Israel from Egypt. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/profane]])

### Sabbaths and idols

The chapter presents keeping Yahweh’s Sabbaths as a sign of his relationship with Israel, and worshiping idols at the high places as breaking that relationship. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sabbath]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/falsegod]], and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/highplaces]]) Verses 26 and 31 refer to the practice of sacrificing children to idols.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Repeated refrain

Each stage of the history in verses 5–22 follows the same pattern: Yahweh gives a command, the people rebel, Yahweh decides to pour out his anger, and then he holds back for the sake of his name. Translating these repeated expressions consistently will help readers see the pattern.

### Verse numbering

In the Hebrew text, verses 45–49 are numbered as 21:1–5. Translations may follow either numbering system.

Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it was more beautiful than any other land]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **man**. He means each of the Israelites in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Each one of you, throw away the detestations of your eye]

Here, **his eye** represents “what he desires.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the detestable things that he desires]

The implication is that the Israelites were not willing to obey what Yahweh told them, not merely that they would not hear him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they were not willing to listen to what I told them and obey it]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the idols of Egypt** after the information about what the Israelites **did not forsake**. Alternate translation: [and they did not forsake the idols of Egypt]

Yahweh is using **I said** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I decided.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verses 13 and 21. Alternate translation: [So I decided to pour]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his **heat**, that is, his anger, were a liquid that he could **pour** on the Israelites. It means that he intended to punish them severely because he was very angry with them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verses 13 and 21. Alternate translation: [to punish them severely because of my anger]

Yahweh is using **to complete my nose against them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to fully express my anger against them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 21. Alternate translation: [to fully unleash my anger against them]

Here, **my name** represents “my reputation.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. This also occurs in verses 14, 22, and 44. Alternate translation: [for the sake of my reputation]

The expression **without being profaned** is a passive verbal form. It refers to the nations treating the name of Yahweh as if it were not holy. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [so that the nations would not treat it as unholy as they watched]
See how you translated this expression in [5:8](../05/08.md). This also occurs in verses 14, 22, and 41.
The word “them” refers to “the descendants of the house of Jacob.”

If your language does not use nouns for the ideas of **statutes** and **judgments**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what I decreed, and what I decided was right]

Quote: אֲשֶׁ֨ר יַעֲשֶׂ֥ה אוֹתָ֛⁠ם הָ⁠אָדָ֖ם וָ⁠חַ֥י בָּ⁠הֶֽם
Note: Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that a person will live if he obeys the statutes and judgments of Yahweh. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. This also occurs in verses 13 and 21. Alternate translation: [If a person obeys them, then he will live by them]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [Any man or woman who does them]

It might seem that the expression **between me and between them** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. This also occurs in verse 20. Alternate translation: [between me and them]

Yahweh is not distinguishing himself from another Yahweh who is not **sanctifying them**. Yahweh is reminding the Israelites that he is the one who sets them apart for himself. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, and that I sanctify them]
See how you translated the similar expression in [6:7](../06/07.md). This also occurs in verses 20, 38, 42, and 44.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his statutes were a path in which the Israelites could **walk**. It means that they did not live in the way that his statutes required. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verses 16, 18, 19, and 21. Alternate translation: [They did not obey my statutes]
See how you translated the similar expression in [3:1](../03/01.md). This also occurs in verses 27, 30, 31, 39, 40, and 44.

The pronouns **who** and **their** refer to the nations, and the pronoun **them** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [before whose eyes I brought the Israelites out]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **lifted** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself swore this oath. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. This also occurs in verses 23 and 25. Alternate translation: [And I myself also lifted]

The implication is that Yahweh swore that he would not bring that generation of Israelites into the land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [swearing that I would not bring that generation of Israelites into the land]

The implication is that Yahweh had promised to give this land to the Israelites. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that I had promised to give them]

The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [I did this because my judgments they rejected]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the **heart** of the Israelites were a person **walking** behind their idols. It means that they eagerly desired to worship their idols. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for they strongly wanted to worship their idols]

Yahweh is using **my eye** to represent himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But I had pity on them]

Yahweh is using **make them a complete end** as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy them completely.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I did not wipe them out]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [their sons and daughters]

The implication is that the Israelites were to keep the Sabbath days holy by setting them apart for Yahweh and by not working on them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And set apart my Sabbaths for me by not working on them]
Yahweh speaks of a person obeying his statutes as if the statutes were a path along which the person walks. Alternate translation: [They did not obey my statutes]

Yahweh speaks of expressing his fury by punishing them as if his fury were a liquid that he poured out on them. See how you translated this in [Ezekiel 20:8](../20/08.md). Alternate translation: [to act against them in my fury]

Yahweh is using **I returned my hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I held back from punishing them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But I refrained from punishing them]

Quote: לְ⁠הָפִ֤יץ אֹתָ⁠ם֙ בַּ⁠גּוֹיִ֔ם וּ⁠לְ⁠זָר֥וֹת אוֹתָ֖⁠ם בָּ⁠אֲרָצֽוֹת
Note: The phrases **to scatter them among the nations** and **to disperse them among the lands** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to scatter them far and wide among all the nations]

Yahweh is using **after the idols of their fathers, their eyes were** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they longed to worship the idols that their ancestors had worshiped.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they longed to worship the idols that their fathers had worshiped]

The implication is that Yahweh allowed the Israelites to follow harmful practices as a punishment for rejecting his good statutes. Some interpreters think Yahweh means that he let them follow the laws and customs of the nations. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [statutes that were not good for them, as a punishment]

Quote: וָ⁠אֲטַמֵּ֤א אוֹתָ⁠ם֙ בְּ⁠מַתְּנוֹתָ֔⁠ם בְּ⁠הַעֲבִ֖יר כָּל פֶּ֣טֶר רָ֑חַם לְמַ֣עַן אֲשִׁמֵּ֔⁠ם לְמַ֨עַן֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יֵֽדְע֔וּ אֲשֶׁ֖ר אֲנִ֥י יְהוָֽה
Note: The first **so that** marks **I might desolate them** as the goal or purpose of **I made them unclean by their gifts**. The second **so that** marks what follows as the goal or purpose of Yahweh making them desolate. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

Yahweh is referring to sacrificing children by burning them in fire in a polite way by using the phrase **making every firstborn of the womb to pass**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [in making every firstborn of the womb to pass through the fire as a sacrifice]
The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Because of all this]

The pronoun **this** refers to the sinful acts that Yahweh describes in the next verse. Some interpreters think it refers back to the rebellions in the wilderness that Yahweh has just described. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Still by what I will now describe, your fathers blasphemed me]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **violation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when they were very unfaithful to me]

Quote: כָל גִּבְעָ֨ה רָמָ֜ה וְ⁠כָל עֵ֣ץ עָבֹ֗ת
Note: The implication is that the Israelites worshiped idols on **every high hill** and under **every leafy tree**, because people thought that those were good places to worship false gods. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [every high hill and every leafy tree, places where people worshiped false gods]

Here, **the anger of their offering** represents “their offering that made me angry.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their offering that provoked me]
See how you translated the similar expression in [6:13](../06/13.md). This also occurs in verse 41.

Quote: וָ⁠אֹמַ֣ר אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֔ם מָ֣ה הַ⁠בָּמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁר־אַתֶּ֥ם הַ⁠בָּאִ֖ים שָׁ֑ם
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And I asked them what the high place was to which they were going]

Quote: מָ֣ה הַ⁠בָּמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁר אַתֶּ֥ם הַ⁠בָּאִ֖ים שָׁ֑ם
Note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the Israelites for worshiping at the high place. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not be going to this high place to worship!]

Quote: וַ⁠יִּקָּרֵ֤א שְׁמָ⁠הּ֙ בָּמָ֔ה עַ֖ד הַ⁠יּ֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּֽה
Note: Yahweh is providing background information to help readers understand why that place was called **Bamah**. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **its name was called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And people have called it Bamah]
The word **Bamah** is the name of a place. It is the same word that is translated as **the high place** earlier in this verse. You could include its meaning in your translation or in a footnote.

Quote: הַ⁠בְּ⁠דֶ֥רֶךְ אֲבֽוֹתֵי⁠כֶ֖ם אַתֶּ֣ם נִטְמְאִ֑ים וְ⁠אַחֲרֵ֥י שִׁקּוּצֵי⁠הֶ֖ם אַתֶּ֥ם זֹנִֽים
Note: Yahweh is using the question form to accuse the Israelites of doing the same evil things that their ancestors did. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You are making yourselves unclean in the way of your fathers, and you are prostituting yourselves after their detestations!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the conduct of the ancestors of the Israelites were a **way**, that is, a path. It means that the Israelites were behaving in the same way as their ancestors. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [By acting just as your fathers did]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if worshiping idols were **prostituting yourselves**. It means that by worshiping other gods the Israelites were being unfaithful to Yahweh, just as a prostitute is unfaithful. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are you being disloyal to me]

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that he will not let the Israelites seek him for guidance. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And I will certainly not be sought by you, house of Israel!]

Quote: חַי אָ֗נִי נְאֻם֙ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֔ה אִם אִדָּרֵ֖שׁ לָ⁠כֶֽם
Note: Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). Yahweh means that he will certainly not let the Israelites seek him for guidance. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [As surely as I live”—the declaration of the Lord Yahweh—“I will certainly not let you seek me for guidance]

Yahweh is using **ascending on your spirit** as a common expression of the culture to mean “coming into your mind.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the thing that comes into your mind]

Yahweh is using **being, it will not be** as a common expression of the culture to mean “it will certainly never happen.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it will certainly never happen]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that you are saying that you want to become like the nations]

Here, **wood and stone** represent “idols made from wood and stone.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to serve idols made from wood and stone]

Quote: חַי אָ֕נִי נְאֻ֖ם אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֑ה אִם לֹ֠א
Note: Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). By saying **if not**, Yahweh means that he will certainly do what he says next. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [As surely as I live”—the declaration of the Lord Yahweh—“it is certain that]

The terms **with a strong hand** and **with an outstretched arm** mean similar things. Both refer to the great power of Yahweh. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. This also occurs in verse 34. Alternate translation: [with very great power]

The expression **heat poured out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. This also occurs in verse 34. Alternate translation: [and with heat that I pour out]

The expression **you were scattered** is a passive verbal form. Yahweh is the one who scattered them. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in which I scattered you]

The implication is that **the wilderness of the peoples** is a desert region among the nations where Yahweh would judge the Israelites, just as he judged their ancestors in the wilderness after they left Egypt. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the desert region among the nations, a wilderness like the one where I judged your ancestors]

Yahweh is using **face to face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “directly and personally.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [directly and personally]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were a shepherd and the Israelites were sheep that he would make **pass under the rod**. A shepherd would hold his rod over his sheep as they passed by in order to count and examine them. It means that Yahweh would carefully examine each of the Israelites. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will carefully examine each one of you]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the covenant were a **bond** that tied the Israelites to him. It means that Yahweh would make the Israelites keep his covenant. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [under the obligation of the covenant]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the rebels were impurities that he would **purge** from metal. It means that he would remove the rebels from among the Israelites. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will remove from among you the rebels]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **sojournings**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [From the land where they have been staying temporarily]

In this verse, the word **he** is singular in form, but it refers to all the rebels as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “he.” Alternate translation: [but to the land of Israel, they will not come]

Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. He does not want the Israelites to serve their idols. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Each man, go ahead and serve his idols, if you insist on doing that]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and afterward keep on serving them, if you are not going to listen to me]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **name** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my name, which is holy]

The implication is that **the mountain of my holiness** is Mount Zion in Jerusalem, where the temple was. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on Mount Zion in Jerusalem, the mountain of my holiness where my temple is, on the mountain of the height of Israel]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **mountain** that is characterized by **height**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the high mountain of Israel]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the Israelites were a sacrifice with **an aroma of pleasing** that he would **accept**. It means that Yahweh would be pleased with the Israelites and accept them, just as he was pleased with sacrifices that people offered to him properly. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [With great pleasure I will accept you]

The expression **I will be sanctified** is a passive verbal form. It means that the nations will see that Yahweh is holy. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [then I will show myself to be holy among you]
See how you translated this expression in [6:9](../06/09.md).
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **evils**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by all the evil things that you did]

The phrases **your evil ways** and **your ruined deeds** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [not according to all the very wicked things that you have done]

Yahweh is using **set your face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “turn and look intently.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [turn and look intently in the direction of Teman]
The words **Teman** and **Darom** are names for the region to the south. Both words mean “south,” so you could also translate them as “the south.”

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the words of Ezekiel were a liquid that he could **drivel**, that is, cause to drip. It means that Ezekiel should speak his prophecy against the south. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and speak your prophecy against Darom]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Judah were **the forest of the field of the Negev**. It means that Yahweh would destroy the people of Judah, just as a fire destroys a forest. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Judah, who are like a forest in the southern land]

Quote: וְ⁠אָֽמַרְתָּ֙ לְ⁠יַ֣עַר הַ⁠נֶּ֔גֶב שְׁמַ֖ע דְּבַר יְהוָ֑ה כֹּֽה אָמַ֣ר אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֡ה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And you shall tell the forest of the Negev to hear the word of Yahweh, for this is what the Lord Yahweh says]

Yahweh is telling Ezekiel to speak to **the forest of the Negev**, which cannot hear him. Ezekiel is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that Yahweh feels very strongly about the judgment that he will bring on Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if Ezekiel were speaking directly to the people of Judah. Alternate translation: [And you shall say to the people of Judah, whom the forest of the Negev represents]

Yahweh is using **Look at me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am about to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to kindle]
The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing **the forest of the Negev**, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his judgment were **a fire** that he would kindle in a forest. It means that he would destroy the people of Judah. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [bringing on you a judgment that is like a fire]

Yahweh is speaking of **a fire** as if it were a living thing that could **eat**. It means that the fire would burn up everything. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it will burn up in you]

Quote: כָל עֵֽץ לַח֩ וְ⁠כָל עֵ֨ץ יָבֵ֤שׁ
Note: Yahweh is referring to all of the trees in the forest by naming two major components, **every fresh tree** and **every dry tree**. Since the forest represents the people of Judah, this means all the people of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every tree without exception]

The expression **will not be quenched** is a passive verbal form. It means that no one will be able to put out the fire. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [No one will be able to extinguish the flame of the blaze]

The terms **flame** and **blaze** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [The raging fire]

Quote: וְ⁠נִצְרְבוּ בָ֥⁠הּ כָּל פָּנִ֖ים מִ⁠נֶּ֥גֶב צָפֽוֹנָ⁠ה
Note: The expression **will be scorched by it** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and it will scorch all faces from the south to the north]

Yahweh is using **all faces** to represent all people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all people]

Yahweh is referring to all of the land by naming two major components, **the south** and **the north**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the whole land]

Yahweh is using **all flesh** to represent all people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all people will see]

The pronoun **it** refers to the fire that Yahweh kindled. Some interpreters think it refers to the forest that the fire burned. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, have caused that fire to burn]
See how you translated this phrase in [4:14](../04/14.md).

# Ezekiel 25 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against the nations around Israel that continues through chapter 32. It contains four short judgment speeches, each against a neighbor that treated Judah’s fall with scorn.

1. Judgment on Ammon (1–7)
    1. Ammon said “Aha!” over the temple, the land, and the exiles (1–5)
    2. Ammon rejoiced with contempt over the land of Israel (6–7)
2. Judgment on Moab (8–11)
3. Judgment on Edom (12–14)
4. Judgment on Philistia (15–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s judgment on nations that scorned Judah

Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines each mocked Judah or took revenge on it when Babylon destroyed the temple and sent the people into exile. Yahweh treats this as an offense against himself and his people, and he declares that he will punish them.

### “You will know that I am Yahweh”

Most of these prophecies end by saying that the punished nation will know that “I am Yahweh.” This shows that the purpose of the judgment is for these nations to recognize Yahweh’s power and authority.

# Ezekiel 26 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against the city of Tyre that continues through [28:19](../28/19.md). It contains four messages from Yahweh, each beginning with “thus says the Lord Yahweh.”

1. Yahweh will judge Tyre because it rejoiced over the fall of Jerusalem (1–6)
2. Nebuchadnezzar will besiege and destroy Tyre (7–14)
3. The rulers of the coastlands will mourn over Tyre (15–18)
    1. The princes of the sea mourn (15–16)
    2. The princes sing a lament over Tyre (17–18)
4. Yahweh will bring Tyre down to the pit (19–21)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [26:17–18](../26/17.md).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Tyre

Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician trading city built on a rocky island just off the coast, with towns that depended on it on the mainland. Other peoples who traded by sea relied on it, so its fall would shock all of the coastlands.

### Mourning for a fallen city

The princes of the sea take off their fine robes, sit on the ground, and sing a funeral song over Tyre. These were common ways to show great grief. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/mourn]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lament]])

### The pit

In verses 19–21, Yahweh speaks of Tyre going down to “the pit” and “the land of the lower parts.” These expressions refer to the place of the dead and indicate that Tyre will be destroyed completely and never exist again. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/pit]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/hades]])

### Changes in how Tyre is referred to

Yahweh speaks to Tyre as “you” but also describes the city as “she” and “her,” sometimes moving from one to the other within a few verses (for example, in verses 3–6 and 17). In the same way, the attackers are called “they” in some verses and “he” (Nebuchadnezzar) in others. Consider whether your language needs to use the same form throughout.

# Ezekiel 27 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a funeral song (lament) over the city of Tyre. It continues the prophecies against Tyre that began in chapter 26. Most of the song describes Tyre as a magnificent trading ship that sinks in the middle of the sea.

  1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to sing a lament over Tyre (1–3)
  2. Tyre is pictured as a beautiful ship (4–11)
    1. The ship is built from the finest materials (4–7)
    2. Men from other cities serve as its crew and soldiers (8–11)
  3. The many nations that traded with Tyre (12–25)
  4. The ship is wrecked in the heart of the seas (26–27)
  5. The sailors and the coastlands mourn over Tyre (28–36)
    1. The sailors weep and mourn (28–31)
    2. The sailors sing their own lament over Tyre (32–36)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [27:3–11](../27/03.md) and [27:25–36](../27/25.md). Verses 12–25 are a list of trading partners written as prose.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Tyre’s sea trade

Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician port whose ships carried goods among many peoples. Verses 12–25 name those peoples and the goods they traded, showing how far Tyre’s trade reached and how rich it had become. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/tyre]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/tarshish]])

### Mourning customs

In verses 30–31 the sailors throw dust on their heads, roll in ashes, shave their heads, and put on sackcloth. These were common ways to show great grief. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/mourn]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lament]], and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/sackcloth]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Tyre as a ship

In verses 4–11 and 25–36, Yahweh speaks of the city of Tyre as if it were a ship, describing its planks, mast, sails, rowers, and cargo. The wreck of the ship represents the destruction of the city. If possible, keep this extended metaphor in your translation, since it runs through most of the chapter.

### Place names and trade goods

The chapter lists many places, peoples, and goods that may be unknown in your culture, and the meaning of some of the Hebrew words is uncertain. You may want to use general terms for goods that your readers would not recognize.

### Past tense for future events

Although the sinking of Tyre had not yet happened, verses 26 and 34 describe it as if it were already past. This shows that it will certainly happen. Consider whether your language would express this with a future form.
See how you translated this expression in [25:1](../25/01.md).
See how you translated the similar expression in [3:16](../03/16.md).
See how you translated **son of man** in [2:1](../02/01.md).

Alternate translation: [sing a mourning song for Tyre]

The prophecy against Egypt and its king concludes in this chapter. Egypt will have its army destroyed, just as happened to so many other nations. # Ezekiel 40 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel begins his description of the restored temple. He describes the outer wall, its gates, the outer courtyard, the inner gates, the inner courtyard, rooms in the courtyards, the altar, and the entryway to the temple building.

1. Yahweh brings Ezekiel to see the temple vision (1–4)
2. The man measures the outer wall and eastern gate (5–16)
3. The man measures the outer court and northern gate (17–27)
4. The man measures the inner court and southern gate (28–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The temple complex

In this chapter, God takes Ezekiel in a vision to see a restored temple in the land of Israel. As Ezekiel describes this restored temple, he assumes that his readers already know what temple complexes in his culture were generally like. He simply starts describing what he sees, starting from the outer wall and moving in. The temple complex he describes has an outer and an inner wall. There is an outer courtyard between the two walls and an inner courtyard within the inner wall. Each of these walls has three gatehouses in it, one each on the north, east, and south sides. The gatehouses in the outer wall protrude into the outer courtyard. The gatehouses in the inner wall also protrude into the outer courtyard. See below for a description of each gatehouse. There were rooms around the outer wall and a pavement in front of them. There were some rooms near the gatehouses through the inner wall. Within the inner courtyard, there was an altar and the temple building itself. The temple building was on the far west side of the temple complex, which is why there were no gates on this side.

### The gatehouses

Each gatehouse had the same structures and measurements. There were steps leading to the gateway itself. Behind the gateway, there was a hallway that passed through the rest of the structure. On each side of the hallway were three recesses with low walls in front of them. For the outer gatehouses, the hallway ended in a porch, which opened onto the outer court. For the inner gatehouses, the porch was in front of the hallway so it too could open onto the outer court. Ezekiel learns the measurements and some of the decorations for all these parts of the gatehouse.

### Ezekiel’s guide

In this chapter, Ezekiel’s guide is called “a man” or “he.” Most scholars think that he is an angel. There are many other stories in this culture about angels who guide a human and show special things to that human. However, Ezekiel does not specify anything about this “man” except that he is bright and shining. Consider how you might refer to this “man” without being too specific.

### Long cubits

In verse 5, Ezekiel states that the man’s measuring stick used long cubits. These cubits were the length of a standard cubit plus one handbreadth. Standard cubits were around 46 centimeters long. A handbreadth was about 8 centimeters. So, these long cubits were around 54 centimeters long. This the length of the cubit that Ezekiel uses throughout the rest of this section. The UST expresses the appropriate measurements in centimeters and meters.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Measurement directions

Ezekiel seems to use the word “width” for the shorter side of a shape and the word “length” for the longer side of a shape. This is particularly clear in [40:49](../40/49.md) and [41:2](../41/02.md). In 40:49, Ezekiel identifies the “length” of the porch as 20 cubits. This measures from the porch from north to south. However, in 41:2, he identifies the “width” of the holy place as 20 cubits. This again measures from north to south. This is not natural in English. Speakers of English usually use the same term for the same compass direction. In this case, an English speaker would probably use “width” for both of these measurements. The ULT follows the Hebrew terms. The UST uses natural English terms. Consider how you might identify directions of measurement in your language.

### Architectural terms and repeated phrases

The exact meaning of some building terms, such as those translated “recess,” “jamb,” “porch,” and “sill,” is uncertain, and translators may use general terms for parts of a gateway. The chapter also repeats expressions such as “around, around” (all the way around), “from here and from there” (on each side), and “the way of the east” (facing east), which should be translated consistently.

### Corrections of the scribes

In this chapter, later scribes provided many corrections in the margins. Sometimes modern translations follow these corrections, and sometimes they do not. The ULT always follows the traditional consonantal text. The UST sometimes follows the corrections in the margins. In these cases, there are notes that explain the alternative reading.

### Alternative readings

There are several places in this chapter where the traditional Hebrew consonants do not make much sense or do not fit with the other descriptions and measurements in this section. In many of these cases, the ancient Greek translation has a reading that makes more sense. Many translations use the ancient Greek translation in these cases. Translation notes identify these specific cases and provide the alternative readings. The UST often, but not always, follows these alternative readings.

# Ezekiel 40 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the final vision of the book, which continues through [chapter 48](../48/01.md). A man who shines like bronze guides Ezekiel through a temple area and measures its walls, gates, courtyards, and rooms.

1. Ezekiel is brought to Israel and meets the man with measuring tools (1–4)
2. The outer courtyard and its gates (5–27)
    1. The wall around the temple area (5)
    2. The east gate (6–16)
    3. The outer courtyard (17–19)
    4. The north gate (20–23)
    5. The south gate (24–27)
3. The inner courtyard and its gates (28–47)
    1. The south gate (28–31)
    2. The east gate (32–34)
    3. The north gate (35–37)
    4. Rooms and tables for preparing sacrifices (38–43)
    5. Rooms for the priests (44–46)
    6. The size of the inner courtyard and the place of the altar (47)
4. The porch of the temple building (48–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The temple in Ezekiel’s vision

In the vision, God shows Ezekiel a [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]] with its [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/court]]s, gates, and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/altar]]. The man tells Ezekiel to report everything he sees to the people of Israel, who were in [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/exile]] and whose temple in Jerusalem had been destroyed.

### Sacrifices and priests

The chapter mentions rooms and tables for preparing the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/burntoffering]], the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/sinoffering]], and the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/guiltoffering]]. It also says that only the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/priest]]s descended from [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/zadok]] may come near to Yahweh to serve him at the altar.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Building terms and measurements

The chapter uses many building terms that may be unfamiliar, such as recesses (small rooms beside a gate), jambs, sills, and porches. It also measures everything in reeds and cubits, and it says that each cubit is a long cubit, one handbreadth longer than the common cubit. Translators may need to use general terms or describe these items, and may want to express the measurements in a way that readers will understand. See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-unknown]] and [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-bdistance]].

### Difficult Hebrew text

The Hebrew text of this chapter is hard to understand in many places. Many of its sentences list measurements in short phrases without verbs, and several verses have textual differences in ancient versions. The ULT follows the Hebrew text closely, but translators may want to follow a translation in their area that makes the meaning clearer. See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-textvariants]].

# Ezekiel 41 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

5. Ezekiel brings messages of hope (34–48)
    * Jerusalem and the temple restored (40–48)

In this chapter, Ezekiel learns about the measurements, decorations, and one piece of furniture for the temple building itself. He also learns about the courtyard around the temple building and a structure to the west of the temple building.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Long cubits

In [40:5](../40/05.md), Ezekiel states that the man’s measuring stick used long cubits. These cubits were the length of a standard cubit plus one handbreadth. Standard cubits were around 46 centimeters long. A handbreadth was about 8 centimeters. So, these long cubits were around 54 centimeters long. This is the length of the cubit that Ezekiel uses throughout this section. The UST expresses the appropriate measurements in centimeters and meters.

### The temple building

The temple building includes two primary rooms, the “nave” (the Holy Place) and the “holy place” (the Most Holy Place). The Holy Place is a rectangle, and the Most Holy Place behind it to the west is a square. The temple building also has a rectangular entryway. There are side chambers whose back walls butt up against the outside wall of the temple building. The temple building sits on a raised platform or foundation. The whole temple building, including the side chambers, is 100 cubits from east to west and 50 cubits from north to south. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]])

### The side chambers

There are three stories of side chambers. It is possible that each story was a single, long chamber that went around the outside of the temple building. It is more likely that each story contained 30 individual rooms that went around the outside of the temple building. There is either a ramp or stairs leading to the higher stories. The higher stories are deeper than the lower stories. This may mean that the temple wall narrowed as it went up. It may mean that the upper stories hung over the lower stories. Scholars are not sure what these side rooms were for. They may have been for storing things.

### The courtyard around the temple building

There was a small courtyard around the temple building. On the north, west, and east sides, there were 20 cubits of space between the edge of the temple building platform and the edges of the courtyard. On the east side of the temple building was the main inner courtyard, which is 100 cubits square according to [40:47](../40/47.md). (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/court]])

### The structure to the west

Ezekiel mentions a “structure” on the west side of the temple building, separated by a small courtyard that is 20 cubits wide. This structure has walls that are five cubits thick. Its exterior measurements are 100 cubits from north to south and 80 cubits from east to west. It is uncertain how tall this building was or what its function was. Most likely, its back wall butted up against the outside wall of the temple complex on the west.

### The altar, or table

In [41:22](../41/22.md), Ezekiel refers to an “altar,” but his guide then calls it a “table.” Scholars guess that this is the same kind of table that the priests used in the tabernacle and temple to present the special bread to God. In this sense, it is like an altar, since priests use it to present things to God. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/altar]])

### The doors

In [41:23–24](../41/23.md), Ezekiel describes the doors that close the entrances into the Holy Place and Most Holy Place. For each entrance, there are two sets of doors. Most likely, one set was at the front of the sill or threshold and the other set was at the back, leaving a small space in between. Each set of doors had two panels, which were connected to the side walls by hinges. In this way, the panels could open by swinging toward the walls. Consider how you might refer to this style of door in your language.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Measurement directions

Ezekiel seems to use the word “width” for the shorter side of a shape and the word “length” for the longer side of a shape. See the introduction to chapter 40 for more information. This is not natural in English. Speakers of English usually use the same term for the same compass direction. The ULT follows the Hebrew terms. The UST uses natural English terms. Consider how you might identify directions of measurement in your language.

### Unknown terms

In this chapter, there are many technical terms for parts of buildings. Often, scholars can guess what these terms mean. However, sometimes scholars are not very sure. This is especially true in [41:6–8](../41/06.md), [16–17](../41/16.md), [21](../41/21.md). The ULT and the UST provide one of several possible ways to understand these verses. You may wish to follow a major translation in your area.

### Terminology for temple rooms

Throughout this chapter, Ezekiel refers to the two important rooms in the temple building. He consistently uses “nave” for the Holy Place. He uses several words for the Most Holy Place, including “inside,” “inner,” “inner house,” and “holy place.” The ULT follows the Hebrew. The UST refers directly to the Most Holy Place.

In this chapter, Ezekiel learns about the measurements, decorations, and one piece of furniture for the temple building itself. He also learns about the courtyard around the temple building and a structure to the west of the temple building.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Long cubits

In [40:5](../40/05.md), Ezekiel states that the man’s measuring stick used long cubits. These cubits were the length of a standard cubit plus one handbreadth. Standard cubits were around 46 centimeters long. A handbreadth was about 8 centimeters. So, these long cubits were around 54 centimeters long. This is the length of the cubit that Ezekiel uses throughout this section. The UST expresses the appropriate measurements in centimeters and meters.

### The temple building

The temple building includes two primary rooms, the “nave” (the Holy Place) and the “holy place” (the Most Holy Place). The Holy Place is a rectangle, and the Most Holy Place behind it to the west is a square. The temple building also has a rectangular entryway. There are side chambers whose back walls butt up against the outside wall of the temple building. The temple building sits on a raised platform or foundation. The whole temple building, including the side chambers, is 100 cubits from east to west and 50 cubits from north to south. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]])

### The side chambers

There are three stories of side chambers. It is possible that each story was a single, long chamber that went around the outside of the temple building. It is more likely that each story contained 30 individual rooms that went around the outside of the temple building. There is either a ramp or stairs leading to the higher stories. The higher stories are deeper than the lower stories. This may mean that the temple wall narrowed as it went up. It may mean that the upper stories hung over the lower stories. Scholars are not sure what these side rooms were for. They may have been for storing things.

### The courtyard around the temple building

There was a small courtyard around the temple building. On the north, west, and east sides, there were 20 cubits of space between the edge of the temple building platform and the edges of the courtyard. On the east side of the temple building was the main inner courtyard, which is 100 cubits square according to [40:47](../40/47.md). (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/court]])

### The structure to the west

Ezekiel mentions a “structure” on the west side of the temple building, separated by a small courtyard that is 20 cubits wide. This structure has walls that are five cubits thick. Its exterior measurements are 100 cubits from north to south and 80 cubits from east to west. It is uncertain how tall this building was or what its function was. Most likely, its back wall butted up against the outside wall of the temple complex on the west.

### The altar, or table

In [41:22](../41/22.md), Ezekiel refers to an “altar,” but his guide then calls it a “table.” Scholars guess that this is the same kind of table that the priests used in the tabernacle and temple to present the special bread to God. In this sense, it is like an altar, since priests use it to present things to God. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/altar]])

### The doors

In [41:23–24](../41/23.md), Ezekiel describes the doors that close the entrances into the Holy Place and Most Holy Place. For each entrance, there are two sets of doors. Most likely, one set was at the front of the sill or threshold and the other set was at the back, leaving a small space in between. Each set of doors had two panels, which were connected to the side walls by hinges. In this way, the panels could open by swinging toward the walls. Consider how you might refer to this style of door in your language.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Measurement directions

Ezekiel seems to use the word “width” for the shorter side of a shape and the word “length” for the longer side of a shape. See the introduction to chapter 40 for more information. This is not natural in English. Speakers of English usually use the same term for the same compass direction. The ULT follows the Hebrew terms. The UST uses natural English terms. Consider how you might identify directions of measurement in your language.

### Unknown terms

In this chapter, there are many technical terms for parts of buildings. Often, scholars can guess what these terms mean. However, sometimes scholars are not very sure. This is especially true in [41:6–8](../41/06.md), [16–17](../41/16.md), [21](../41/21.md). The ULT and the UST provide one of several possible ways to understand these verses. You may wish to follow a major translation in your area.

# Ezekiel 42 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

5. Ezekiel brings messages of hope (34–48)
    * Jerusalem and the temple restored (40–48)

In this chapter, Ezekiel learns about rooms that are grouped together into two buildings, one to the northwest of the temple building and one to the southwest of the temple building. He learns that these rooms are for the sacred offerings and clothing. Finally, Ezekiel learns the dimensions of the outer wall of the whole temple complex.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The chambers

There are two buildings full of chambers, one to the north and one to the south of the structure and courtyard to the west of the temple building. Scholars agree that these buildings are three stories high, and that the highest story’s rooms are smaller than the rooms in the lower stories. Scholars disagree on many other things about how these buildings were constructed. There is a walkway next to each building, but it is not certain which side of the building it is on. There is a wall near the walkway, but it is not certain exactly where it runs. There are “ledges” on each building, but it is not certain exactly what they look like or what their function is. It is clear that these buildings were for the priests to use while they were interacting with holy places and things. When the meaning of a description is uncertain, consider following a major translation in your area or the reading represented by the UST.

### Holy and common

In this chapter, there is a strong distinction between what is holy, or set apart for God, and what is common, or ordinary. Holy and common places, things, and people are not supposed to mix. Both the wall around the temple complex and the two buildings in this chapter help separate what is holy from what is common. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/holy]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Alternative readings

There are several places in this chapter where the standard written Hebrew text we have today does not make much sense. Instead, a correction written by a scribe or an ancient translation sometimes makes more sense. In these cases, the notes provide the alternative reading provided by the correction or ancient translation. Consider following a major translation in your area or the reading represented by the UST. # Ezekiel 43 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

5. Ezekiel brings messages of hope (34–48)
    * Jerusalem and the temple restored (40–48)

In this chapter, Ezekiel sees Yahweh return to the temple. Yahweh then speaks to him. He tells Ezekiel about what the Israelites did wrong in the past what he needs to tell them now about this temple. Then, he tells Ezekiel about the altar and the sacrifices required to consecrate it.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh returns

In this chapter, Ezekiel sees Yahweh’s glory arrive at and enter the temple. This is important in the book of Ezekiel because in chapter 10, Yahweh leaves the temple. When Yahweh leaves it is judgment against the Israelites. So, when Yahweh returns, it is repairing the relationship between the Israelites and Yahweh. Ezekiel says that Yahweh’s glory looked like what he had seen previously. These previous visions are in [Ezekiel 1](../01/01.md) and [8](../08/01.md). See those chapters for help in translating terms and ideas in [43:1–5](../43/01.md).

### The altar

In [43:13–17](../43/13.md), the sacrificial altar for the temple is described. Much of this description is difficult for scholars to understand. There are three important decisions that translators need to make. First, is the altar made out of three sections or just two? It is clear that the altar is made up of square sections that are stacked on top of each other. The higher section is two cubits narrower than the section it sits on. What is not clear is whether there are two or three of these sections. The UST models an altar with three sections. Second, how many gutters are there on this altar? It is clear that there is a gutter around the base of the altar. This gutter collects the blood from the animals. This may be the only gutter, or there may be a second gutter at the edge of the highest section of the altar. The UST models an altar with two gutters. Third, [43:17](../43/17.md) indicates that one of the sections is 14 cubits on each side. Which section is this? It may be the highest section or the middle section. The UST models an altar which has a 14-cubit square highest section. The altar also has a square area on the top for burning the sacrifices and horns at the four corner of this square area. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/altar]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Who speaks in 43:13–17?

In [43:13–17](../43/13.md), there is information about the shape and measurements of the altar. It is unclear who is gives this information. It could be the “man” who has guided Ezekiel previously. It could be Ezekiel himself, writing down what he learned. It could be Yahweh speaking from the temple. Since it is Yahweh who speaks in both the section before and the section after, the UST indicates that Yahweh speaks 43:13–17.

### Pronouns in 43:19–27

In [43:19–27](../43/19.md), Yahweh uses “you” in both singular and plural, “they,” and “he.” The word “you” in the singular refers to Ezekiel, and in the plural it refers to all the Israelites. The pronoun “he” probably refers to any person Ezekiel commissions to do a task. The pronoun “they” probably refers to the priests. The UST models this interpretation. However, some scholars argue that “they,” like “he,” could refer to any person more generally. It is also possible that “you,” while referring to Ezekiel, might mean that Ezekiel needs to have someone else do something instead of doing it himself. Consider following a major translation in your area, or you could follow the interpretation represented by the UST. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-pronouns]])
